nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What did studies highlight regarding vulnerabilities in resource management systems?
nodes.answer: Studies highlighted the vulnerabilities and gaps in existing systems and proposed strategies for enhancing resilience and sustainability in the face of future crises.
nodes.paragraph: Water, energy and food resource management faces challenges such as limited accessibility, increas- ing demand and risks from the international market. Considering an anticipated global population of about 9 billion by 2050, food and energy production are expected to increase by 70% and 50%, respectively, while water demand will increase by 55%. Half of the global population is predicted to experience water stress by 2050 (UNDP, 2015). Limited access to land and water will lead to trade- offs and competition between food and energy production. These challenges have been exacerbated by the pandemic, with directly impacts on both water and food contamination, and indirectly effects unemployment, social unrest and disrup- tions in supply chains. Low- and middle-income states are particularly suscepti- ble to these impacts (Diffenbaugh et al., 2020). Studies highlighted the vulnerabilities and gaps in the existing systems and proposed strategies for enhancing resilience and sustainability in the face of simi- lar future crises (Cheshmehzangi, 2020; Deaton & Deaton, 2020). The pandemic served as a wake-up call for the importance of integrated approaches to address the interdependencies between the water, energy and food segments.

nodes.question: What is emphasized as essential for the development and safety assessment of next-generation reactors?
nodes.answer: Robust frameworks and computational tools, such as codes, standards, and high-performance computing, are emphasized as essential.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What is the primary objective of the article discussed in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The primary objective of the article is to identify the relevant dimensions of energy vulnerability and resilience and to empirically map the positioning of economies concerning these dimensions in the context of EU Member States.
nodes.paragraph: No Title Available DOI: DOI not available FullTextURL:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40812-025-00340-9 Journal of Industrial and Business Economics https://doi.org/10.1007/s40812-25-340-9 Abstract This paper analyses energy vulnerability and resilience in the EU. First, a compre - hensive review of the relevant literature is carried out, discussing key concepts and indicators used to assess countries relative positioning vis- -vis energy shocks. Second, we rely on a large set of indicators (i.e., share of energy intensive indus - tries, import dependency and market concentration, productive and technological capabilities in the renewables domain, policy efforts to increase energy resilience) to provide a thorough mapping of EU Member States positioning in terms of en - ergy vulnerability and resilience. Third, we assess industrial and energy policy ac - tions put in place at both the EU and the national level, highlighting relevant het - erogeneities and discussing whether policy efforts are consistent with the degree of vulnerability of Member States. Keywords Energy vulnerability Energy resilience Europe Industrial policy JEL classification C38 O13 Q43 Q48 1 Introduction Since the explosion of the war in Ukraine, accelerating the energy transition has become a top policy priority in Europe (Tagliapietra et al., 2023 ).

nodes.question: What challenges do EU Member States face regarding their response to energy vulnerability?
nodes.answer: EU Member States face significant heterogeneities in their economic structures and capabilities, resulting in uneven resource allocation where they are needed most, exacerbating their structural vulnerabilities and complicating coordinated policy responses.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Climate resilience|Resilience planning for energy infrastructure_qna_004
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the two intertwined concepts discussed in the paper regarding energy vulnerability and resilience?
nodes.answer: The two concepts are energy vulnerability and energy resilience, which are interconnected but not overlapping, reflecting the different resources needed to minimize socio-economic costs and accelerate post-shock adjustment in the face of energy shocks.
nodes.paragraph: A paradigmatic example is the RePowerEU plan, which intends to make the EU carbon-neutral by 2050 and decouple from Russian energy imports by 2027. Nonetheless, as the interdependencies along energy-related supply chains start being weaponized (Drezner et al., 2021 ), Europe had to experience first- hand its structural vulnerability (Caravella et al., 2024 ). While the supply of energy from renewable sources is still grossly inadequate to meet the demand stemming from a rather energy-intensive manufacturing base, dependence on imported fossil fuels proved to be significantly high (Carfora et al., 2022 ). On the other hand, diver - sification capacity turns out to be asymmetrical across Member States and, in many cases, not up to the challenge (Celi et al., 2022 ). Indeed, what explains such a policy urgency are the potentially heavy socio- economic consequences of energy shocks. Growing energy bills may jeopardize competitiveness and growth, turning into industry-level crises, unemployment and rising inequalities. The less diversification capacity and resources are available to put in place both short- and long-term policy actions, the stronger and more persistent such effects can be.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Clean energy|Climate resilience|Resilience planning for energy infrastructure_qna_005
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What are the two key concepts discussed in relation to energy vulnerability and resilience in the EU?
nodes.answer: The two key concepts are energy vulnerability and energy resilience. These concepts are intertwined but not overlapping, as they both relate to how entities cope with energy shocks while having different resources to mitigate their socio-economic costs.
nodes.paragraph: The scale of the problem has been highlighted by the significant amount of resources that the EC and most member states have to put on the ground, since February 2022, to protect incomes and support businesses facing skyrocket - ing energy prices (Sgaravatti et al., 2023 ). Yet, these efforts risk being frustrated by the peculiar flaw that has already weakened the EU economy during recent crises (i.e., the GFC and the Covid-19 crisis): its internal divergence and the parallel lack of cooperation/coordination in terms of both fiscal and industrial policy (Celi et al., 2020 ). In the case of the energy crises, this problem is further exacerbated by the fact that EU economies face significantly heterogeneous conditions (Celi et al., 2018 , 2020 ; Massetti & Exadaktylos, 2022 ; Rhinard, 2019 ). As some member states are characterized by a relatively large share of energy-intensive industries, others have a more service-oriented industrial structure. Likewise, while in some member states the share of energy stemming from renewable sources has already reached remark - able levels, in others imported oil and gas represents the fundamental source of sup - ply.

nodes.answer: The main objectives are to review key concepts and indicators related to energy vulnerability and resilience, map the positioning of EU member states concerning these factors, and assess EU and national policy actions aimed at reducing vulnerability and increasing resilience to energy shocks.
